The 'Physics' in Babylon.js is at the inexcusably 'my first game engine' level of incompetence. Velocity and acceleration treated as if they have the same dimensions; no understanding of world time, causing issues across different frame rates.

I think Havoc physics will be a very welcome addition... As a technical 3D artist, Babylon has been a great way to dive into web dev, and it parallels with standard game engines just enough that I can easily find my way around the documentation.
Babylon is amazing, the documentation and backwards compatibility is quite something. Just finished a project with it, while the learning curve is steep, it doesn't blindside you.

My wife found that ThreeJS breaks backwards compatibility a lot, while Babylon is exactly the opposite. Babylon also has vastly superior documentation and doesn't seem to suffer from lag spikes as much. However, it's an oldschool API and requires quite a bit of learning; also it's three times the size of ThreeJS.

I had high hopes for babylon.js... My gripes: no 'preferred navigation feel', doesn't care for real-world physics scale, setting up a default test scene is kludgy, and I never found any active community using it outside MS release announcements.

three.js seems more well known/established than babylon... I went with babylon and I'm glad I did. Better performance and the object names and concepts seemed easier to follow and less obtuse. They are extremely diligent about working through bugs on github.
Babylon seemed much more approachable than three for basic stuff (a box and a camera). However there is a lot more written about three than Babylon.

I switched from Three to Babylon two years ago... Babylon has a compact, active set of devs (I've made bug reports and seen the fix in the next nightly build multiple times)... Babylon is more of a 'game engine' than a '3D engine' with built-in subsystems for bone animations, audio triggers, etc.
Babylon.js is an amazing framework. The 3d concepts are ingrained into the API and framework. The ability to read 3d model data from Blender and things just work is awesome.
The impressive thing about Babylon.js is Spector, a fully functional WebGL debugger extension in Chrome which makes 3D development on the web so much easier, works with Three.js too!

I would say it is more of a game engine, especially compared to three.js. Babylon.js supports physics plug-ins and collisions, has an action manager, great docs and community support; posted a question in the forum and got a fix in hours.

Babylon.js is based on the Babylon Toolkit for Silverlight, and includes significantly more features than Three.js, including sprite support and other 2d-graphics functionality. Works in all 3 major browsers, performs best in Firefox, not IE10.
It seems to be pretty heavy on object allocation, e.g. BABYLON.Vector3.prototype.add creates a new Vector3 each time, unlike gl-matrix's in-place operations, risking GC pressure.
The next version (1.2) will remove the pressure on GC by using in-place operators and by reusing more entities.
Love the work being done with BabylonJS, those guys rock, despite the limitations of the 3D Web APIs versus native ones their demos always surprise me in some fashion.
This has so many more capabilities than Three.js and the gap seems to be growing.
Babylon is awesome! I just started writing a game with it. The integration with TypeScript works well and there also are very fun things like React-BabylonJS.

I decided to start developing a 3rd-person MMORPG using Babylon v4.0... after investing far too much time I came to question why I was bothering with a strictly web-based engine... halted dev on the babylon version and begun porting to Godot. Babylon is a great choice for web-based 3d content, but for a significant game I'd recommend a proper game engine from the start.

demos look quite nice but wow they take a long time to load, took about 5 minutes to download 50mb for a short scene, makes me wonder if download times are going to be a limiting factor in webgl games.
To avoid having too long loading time, we have support for incremental loading. But we definitely need to work on optimizing the size of our scene format also.
